The company, the services, the backends and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You run the observability platform at Larchfield Bank, a fictional bank. All services send OTLP to a gateway Collector that exports traces to two backends: the in-house tracing store and a vendor used by the fraud team. During this morning's peak the gateway was OOM-killed three times and traces went missing.
handover: Traces pipeline: receivers otlp; processors batch; exporters otlp/inhouse and otlp/vendor, sharing one queue setting.
The vendor's endpoint was slow all morning. Some spans carry user.email as an attribute.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the map shows each component and its status in words.
Move on a check-in at a time. A decision comes to you at each check-in; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Check-in 2: at the 10:30 peak the gateway is OOM-killed again with 40 seconds of traces in memory; the fraud team loses traces for a disputed payment.
Check-in 3: the fraud team's alerting goes silent; a card-testing attack runs for an hour before anyone notices.
Check-in 4: the privacy audit finds 3 million customer emails in the vendor's trace store; the bank must report it.

effects.log: Check-in 1: the next peak is at 10:30.
Check-in 2: the vendor is slow again.
Check-in 3: the privacy officer asks about user.email.

memPrompt.title: The gateway keeps getting OOM-killed
memPrompt.context: The pod's memory limit is 2 GiB.

choices.label: Add memory_limiter as the first processor (limit about 80% of 2 GiB, with a spike allowance), batch after it, and run three gateway replicas behind a load balancer

effects.log: memory_limiter first, batch second, three replicas.

choices.feedback: memory_limiter refuses data before memory runs out, so clients retry instead of the Collector dying with everything in it.

choices.label: Raise the pod's memory limit to 8 GiB

effects.log: The limit is raised to 8 GiB.

choices.feedback: It takes longer to die; with a slow backend the buffer still grows until it does.

choices.label: Add memory_limiter after batch to protect the exporters
choices.feedback: After batch, data is already buffered in memory before the limiter sees it; the OOMs continue.

fanPrompt.title: One slow backend
fanPrompt.context: The vendor endpoint is slow; its full queue holds memory the in-house exporter needs.

choices.label: Give each exporter its own sending_queue sized for its backend and retry_on_failure with a max elapsed time; use a file-backed persistent queue for the in-house store

effects.log: Each exporter has its own queue and retries; in-house survives restarts.

choices.feedback: Each exporter has its own queue and retry policy, so one slow backend fills only its queue, and a persistent queue survives restarts.

choices.label: Raise both queues to 50,000
choices.feedback: More buffer for the vendor means more memory held; the limiter will refuse data sooner for everyone.

choices.label: Remove the vendor exporter: the fraud team can use the in-house store
choices.feedback: The fraud team's detections run only in the vendor; removing it blinds them.

piiPrompt.title: Emails in span attributes
piiPrompt.context: user.email reaches both backends, including the vendor.

choices.label: Add an attributes processor that deletes user.email (and hashes user.id) after memory_limiter and before batch, so no exporter receives it; ask the teams to stop setting it
choices.feedback: Processor order matters: redaction before batch and export means no backend ever receives the value.

choices.label: Ask the vendor to drop the field on their side

effects.log: The vendor is asked to drop it.

choices.feedback: The data still leaves the bank before anything removes it.

choices.label: Leave it: the vendor contract covers personal data
choices.feedback: Personal data the bank does not need is still sent to a third party.

reflection.question: Write the change record: why the gateway died, how the pipelines are ordered now, and how each backend is isolated.

parts.label: Order
parts.criteria: memory_limiter first, then attributes redaction, then batch, then exporters.
parts.modelAnswer: Processors run in order: memory_limiter refuses data before memory runs out, attributes removes user.email, then batch.

parts.label: Exporters
parts.criteria: Own queue and retry policy per exporter; persistent queue in-house; three replicas.
parts.modelAnswer: Each exporter has its own sized queue and retries, the in-house one persistent, behind three gateway replicas.

scoring.modelReasoning: Collector processors run in the order a pipeline lists them: memory_limiter first, so data is refused (and clients retry) before memory runs out; then transforms such as attribute redaction; then batch. Each exporter has its own sending queue and retry policy, so a slow backend fills only its own queue; persistent queues survive restarts, and horizontal scaling spreads load. Removing a backend or raising memory hides the design problem.
